To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the EMG signal is a result of the summation of action potentials of muscle fibres, that these action potentials are generated in response to afferent input to the spinal cord, that the afferent input is a function of the muscle fibre activation and that the EMG is a result of a summation of the muscle fibre action potentials.
the surface EMG signal reflects the recruitment and rate coding of motor units.

the surface EMG spectrum of the biceps bruchii muscle is determined by the recruitment and firing rate of the motor units, as well as the size of the motor units and the spread of the action potential to the surface electrode.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and evaluation of a model of muscle activation and its associated surface EMG.
the development of models to link the electrical activity of muscle fibres to the surface EMG and to the underlying motor unit activation.
the development of models that link muscle activation and muscle force generation to the surface EMG signal.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a decrease in the size of the motor units leads to an increase in the high frequency component of the EMG power spectrum.
the model is consistent with experimental findings and provides a plausible explanation for the EMG power spectra observed in patients with neuromuscular disorders.

the EMG power spectrum reflects motor unit recruitment and rate coding, and is sensitive to the number of motor units activated, the size of the motor units activated, and the rate of firing of the motor units.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a muscle with an abnormal EMG power spectrum is likely to have an abnormal recruitment and rate coding pattern.
the frequency shifts in EMG power spectra are due to changes in motor unit size and recruitment order, and not due to changes in the firing rates of the motor units.
the EMG signal can be interpreted as a measure of motor unit activity and that the power spectra can be used to quantify this activity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a single motor unit can be responsible for a large portion of the EMG signal.
the EMG power spectrum is a function of motor unit recruitment and rate coding, and that these two mechanisms can be separated by the analysis of the EMG power spectra.
a single motor unit can be represented by a single EMG signal.
